params.question: In a medico-legal examination to confirm pregnancy, which of the following is classified as a positive sign?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Uterine enlargement is a probable sign — it can also be caused by conditions such as uterine fibroids.

answers.text: Foetal heart sounds detected by the examiner

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Foetal heart sounds detected by the examiner are a positive (diagnostic) sign. Along with examiner-felt foetal movements and ultrasound visualisation of a live foetus, only positive signs support a definitive medico-legal opinion of pregnancy.
A positive hCG test is classified as probable, not positive. Ectopic pregnancy or gestational trophoblastic disease can produce positive results without a viable intrauterine pregnancy.
Goodell's sign is a probable sign appearing around 6–8 weeks. Though strongly suggestive, cervical softening has other possible explanations and does not confirm pregnancy definitively.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three-tier classification: presumptive signs are subjective symptoms, probable signs are objective but have alternative explanations, and only positive signs (foetal heart sounds, examiner-felt movements, ultrasound) are diagnostic.
Well done. In medico-legal practice, only positive signs — foetal heart sounds, examiner-felt foetal movements, and ultrasound visualisation — support a definitive opinion that a woman is pregnant.

params.question: After a vasectomy performed under the National Family Planning Programme, when should the man be considered sterile?

answers.text: Immediately after the procedure, once the wound heals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The man is not sterile immediately. Residual sperm persist in the reproductive ducts distal to the ligation site and can cause fertilisation.

answers.text: After two weeks, when local inflammation resolves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Two weeks is insufficient. Sperm can survive in the vas deferens and ejaculatory ducts for weeks after the procedure.

answers.text: Only after semen analysis at twelve weeks confirms azoospermia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Residual sperm remain in the ducts after vasectomy. Azoospermia must be confirmed by semen analysis at approximately twelve weeks post-procedure. Until then, the man can still father a child — a point central to medicolegal negligence claims.

answers.text: After completing three months of hormonal suppression therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vasectomy is a mechanical procedure that blocks sperm transit. No hormonal suppression therapy is used or required after the procedure.

overallFeedback.feedback: After vasectomy, residual sperm persist in the reproductive ducts. Sterility is confirmed only by semen analysis showing azoospermia at approximately twelve weeks. Failure to counsel about this delay is a common basis for negligence claims.
Correct. This twelve-week confirmation requirement is a key medicolegal point — failed sterilisation claims often arise because couples were not counselled about the delay to azoospermia.

interactions.label: At autopsy, a young woman who died from a suspected criminal abortion shows frot

params.question: At autopsy, a young woman who died from a suspected criminal abortion shows frothy blood in the heart chambers and chemical burns of the endometrium. Which method of criminal abortion best explains these findings?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral abortifacients like quinine produce gastric mucosal irritation and systemic toxicity at autopsy, not chemical burns of the endometrium.

answers.text: Instrumentation with unsterile metal objects through the cervix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Instrumentation with objects like knitting needles or bicycle spokes causes cervical lacerations and uterine perforation — a mechanical injury pattern, not chemical burns.
Misoprostol acts pharmacologically on uterine smooth muscle to induce contractions. It does not cause chemical burns of the endometrium, even when taken without medical supervision.

answers.text: Introduction of soap solution or lysol into the uterine cavity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Caustic fluids such as soap solution or lysol introduced directly into the uterus cause chemical peritonitis and endometrial burns. Frothy blood in the heart chambers indicates a fatal air embolism — a recognised complication when fluids are forced into the uterine cavity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each criminal abortion method leaves a distinct forensic pattern: caustic fluids → chemical burns and air embolism; instrumentation → cervical lacerations and uterine perforation; oral abortifacients → gastric mucosal irritation. Matching the injury pattern to the method is essential in medicolegal investigation.

Well done. The combination of chemical burns and air embolism is the forensic signature of intrauterine instillation of caustic substances — a key finding in investigating deaths due to criminal abortion.

interactions.label: The PC&PNDT Act prohibits all forms of prenatal diagnostic techniques in India.

params.question: The PC&PNDT Act prohibits all forms of prenatal diagnostic techniques in India.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The PC&PNDT Act does not ban all prenatal diagnostics. It permits them for legitimate medical indications such as detecting chromosomal abnormalities, genetic disorders, and metabolic conditions. The Act specifically prohibits using these techniques for sex determination or sex selection, and mandates registration, Form F documentation for every antenatal ultrasound, and two-year record-keeping.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The PC&PNDT Act does not ban prenatal diagnostics altogether. It permits techniques such as ultrasound, amniocentesis, and chorionic villus sampling for detecting chromosomal abnormalities, genetic disorders, and metabolic conditions. What the Act specifically prohibits is the use of any prenatal or pre-conception technique for sex determination or sex selection.

params.question: A 4-month-old infant is found dead in the crib with no external injuries. Autopsy reveals only non-specific thymic petechiae and pulmonary congestion. What is the most appropriate next step before diagnosing Sudden Infant Death Syndrome?

answers.text: Conduct a thorough death scene investigation and review the clinical history

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. SIDS is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring three independent components: a complete autopsy, a review of the clinical history, and a death scene investigation. The scene investigation — checking sleeping position, bedding, co-sleepers, and surveillance footage — is critical because homicidal smothering produces identical autopsy findings.

answers.text: Diagnose SIDS based on the non-contributory autopsy findings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SIDS cannot be diagnosed on autopsy findings alone. Non-specific thymic petechiae and pulmonary congestion are found in both natural SIDS and homicidal smothering — the autopsy cannot distinguish between the two.

answers.text: Attribute the death to accidental suffocation from prone sleeping position

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While prone sleeping is a known risk factor for SIDS, attributing the death to any specific cause without completing the full investigation triad is premature and could mask a homicide.

answers.text: Request genetic screening for inherited cardiac channelopathies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Genetic screening may be relevant in selected cases, but the immediate priority is completing the diagnostic triad — autopsy, clinical history review, and death scene investigation — before considering ancillary investigations.

overallFeedback.feedback: SIDS is strictly a diagnosis of exclusion. All three components — complete autopsy, clinical history review, and death scene investigation — must fail to identify a cause of death. Since homicidal smothering can mimic SIDS at autopsy, the scene investigation is indispensable.

Well done. The three-pronged approach — autopsy, clinical history, and scene investigation — is the cornerstone of SIDS diagnosis. Remember: repeated unexplained infant deaths in the same family should raise a red flag for possible homicide, not coincidence.
